title: Patient-Specific In Vivo Gene Editing to Treat a Rare Genetic Disease
one_line: A bespoke, patient-specific in vivo base-editing therapy was designed, manufactured and dosed in an infant with severe CPS1 deficiency, a rare urea-cycle disorder.
key_claims: The team built an N-of-1 lipid nanoparticle-delivered base editor targeting the patient's own CPS1 variant and moved from diagnosis to dosing within months.
The infant received sequential escalating doses in vivo, with the therapy directed to hepatocytes as the relevant target tissue.
Post-dosing the patient tolerated increased dietary protein and required less nitrogen-scavenger medication, consistent with partial metabolic correction.
No serious treatment-related adverse events attributable to the editing agent were reported over the short follow-up.
The authors present the case as a template for rapid, individualized in vivo gene-editing therapies for ultra-rare variants.
limitations: A single patient with short follow-up, so efficacy and durability cannot be established.
On-target editing efficiency in liver could not be directly measured in the living patient.
Clinical improvement is confounded by concurrent standard metabolic management and normal infant growth/development.
Long-term safety, including off-target editing and immune responses to the delivery vehicle, remains unknown.
The regulatory and manufacturing path used may not generalize or scale to other patients or centers.
open_questions: Does the metabolic benefit persist as the child grows and liver mass turns over?
What is the actual per-allele editing efficiency achieved in hepatocytes, and is redosing needed?
Can the bespoke design-to-dose pipeline be reproduced for other variants and diseases within a comparable timeline and cost?
